cards.title: 2.1.1 Motion, Frame of Reference and Coordinate System
body: Birds fly, fish swim, blood flows through veins and arteries and cars move.
Atoms, molecules, planets, and stars are all in motion.
Buses transport people from one place to another.
Aeoroplanes fly from one place to another.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Distance and Displacement
body: A learner said to his friend that he walks about 2 km from his home to school.
In everyday language, the terms distance and displacement are used in the same sense.
Definitely he is 200 m – 60 m = 140 m east of his initial position.
The change in position during a given time interval is called **displacement**.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Speed and Velocity
body: In everyday language, people use the terms speed and velocity interchangeably just as they use the words distance and displacement.
In physics speed and velocity have different meanings.
**Speed** is defined as the distance travelled per unit time.
The **SI unit for speed** is the metres per second (m/s or m.s-1).

cards.title: 2.1.4 Acceleration
body: For example, a car may start from rest, speed up to 60 km/h, remain at that velocity for some time, then slow down and finally stop.
A body moving with changing velocity is said to have acceleration.
Motion in which the velocity changes is known as **non-uniform or accelerated motion**.
**Acceleration** is the rate-of-change of velocity.

cards.title: 2.1.5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion
body: Sometimes an accelerating object will change its velocity by the same amount each second.
An object with a constant acceleration should not be confused with an object with a constant velocity.
If an object is changing its velocity – whether by a constant amount or a varying amount it is said to be accelerating.
An object with a constant velocity is not accelerating.

cards.title: 2.1.6 Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion
body: For motions with constant acceleration the average acceleration is equal to the constant acceleration.
Replacing aav by the constant acceleration a in Eq.
The average velocity can be calculated as: (6 m/s + 8 m/s + 10 m/s + 12 m/s + 14 m/s)/5 10 m/s, or in a simple way as (6.0 m/s + 14 m/s )/2 = 10 m/s.
Solution: The velocity of the car, found from Eq.

cards.title: 2.1.7 Freely Falling Objects
body: An object thrown upwards falls back down because there are forces of gravity and air resistance acting on it.
In air, heavy objects fall faster than very light objects: in a vacuum, they fall at the same rate.
The difference is due to the effect of air resistance being greater on light bodies than on heavy ones.
A standard demonstration to show the rate of fall is that of a coin and paper demonstration.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: A person walks $$200\text{ m}$$ to the East, then turns around and walks $$60\text{ m}$$ to the West. What is the magnitude of the person's displacement?

steps.text: **Given:** Initial displacement $$x_1 = +200\text{ m}$$ (taking East as positive), subsequent displacement $$x_2 = -60\text{ m}$$ (West).
**Formula:** $$\Delta x = x_1 + x_2$$
**Substitution:** $$\Delta x = 200\text{ m} + (-60\text{ m}) = 140\text{ m}$$.
**Final Result:** The magnitude of the displacement is **$$140\text{ m}$$**.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Zahra travels by car a total distance of $$640\text{ km}$$ in $$8\text{ h}$$. What was her average speed?

steps.text: **Given:** Total distance $$s = 640\text{ km}$$, total time taken $$t = 8\text{ h}$$.
**Formula:** $$v_{av} = \frac{s}{t}$$
**Substitution:** $$v_{av} = \frac{640\text{ km}}{8\text{ h}} = 80\text{ km/h}$$.
**Final Result:** The average speed is **$$80\text{ km/h}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The speedometer of a car gives a reading of the car's:
cards.why:
**Given:** Speedometer reading of a moving car.

**Formula:** The speedometer shows the rate of travel at one specific moment in time without indicating direction.

**Substitution:** Speed at a specific instant is called instantaneous speed. Velocity requires direction, and average values require an interval, which a speedometer does not calculate directly.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Instantaneous speed**.

cards.title: 2.2.1 Distance-time Graph for Motion with Uniform Velocity
body: A body travelling with uniform velocity covers equal distances, in a specified direction, in equal times.
For example, a motor cycle moving at a uniform velocity of 5m/s travels a distance of 5 m in 1 s, 10 m in 2 s, 15 m in 3 s and so on.
In time ‘t’ seconds it would cover a distance of ‘5t’ m.
When the distance travelled by a body is plotted against time the graph obtained is a distance-time graph.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Velocity-time Graph for Motion with Uniform Velocity
body: The velocity-time graph for motion with uniform velocity is a horizontal line, that is, a line parallel to the time axis.
The slope in a velocity-time graph represents acceleration.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Distance-time Graph for Motion with Uniform Acceleration
body: As time passes the distance increases faster and faster.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Velocity-time Graph for Motion with Uniform Acceleration
body: The acceleration of an object can be positive, zero or negative.
During the 4 s the velocity decreases uniformly from 40 m/s to zero.
The velocity is zero at the highest point.
The maximum height is found from the area of the triangle OPQ.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An object moving under the influence of gravity alone is said to be in:
cards.why:
**Given:** Object moving solely under gravitational force.

**Formula:** By definition, an object moving under gravity without air resistance or other forces is experiencing free fall.

**Substitution:** Since the only force is gravity, the object accelerates downward at $$g$$. This motion is defined as free fall.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **B. Free fall**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The velocity-time graph of an object moving with a uniform constant velocity is a:

options.C: C. Horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis
options.D: D. Sloping straight line passing through the origin

cards.why:
**Given:** Uniform constant velocity motion.

**Formula:** On a $$v-t$$ graph, the y-axis represents velocity. If velocity is constant, its value does not change over time.

**Substitution:** A constant y-value results in a flat horizontal line with a slope of zero, parallel to the horizontal time axis.

**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The velocity-time graph of an object moving with a uniform constant velocity is a:

steps.text: **Given:** Uniform constant velocity motion.
**Formula:** On a $$v-t$$ graph, the y-axis represents velocity. If velocity is constant, its value does not change over time.
**Substitution:** A constant y-value results in a flat horizontal line with a slope of zero, parallel to the horizontal time axis.
**Final Result:** The correct option is **C. Horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis**.

cards.answer: C. Horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: On a velocity–time graph, the area under the graph gives the ____.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Area = velocity × time.

**Step 2:** Velocity × time = displacement.

**Step 3:** The slope of a v–t graph gives acceleration.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

glossary.meaning: Kinematics is the description of how objects move and dynamics deals with why objects move as they do.
Motion is a continuous change of position (or location) with time.
Displacement is the final (new) position minus the initial (old) position.
Speed is defined as the distance travelled per unit time.
Acceleration is the rate-of-change of velocity.
Distance is the total length of the path followed.

tips.text: Every body in the universe is in motion.
Motion is a continuous change of position (or location) with time.
The position of an object is its location relative to a reference point.
As an object moves it covers a certain distance.
Distance is the total length of the path followed.
A vector quantity related to distance is the displacement of a body in motion.
Displacement is the straight line distance in a specific direction.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time whereas velocity is the displacement per unit time.
Speed is a scalar quantity whereas velocity is a vector quantity.

When the velocity of a body remains constant, then the motion is known as uniform motion. However, when the velocity changes in magnitude or direction, the motion is said to be accelerated motion and the object possesses accelerations.
Motion in one dimension: v=u+at s=ut+½at² v²=u²+2as s = displacement. Free fall: a=±g. v–t slope = a; area under v–t = displacement.

questions.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
questions.answer: Speed is how fast (scalar); velocity is speed in a given direction (vector).
why: Speed = distance ÷ time – size only.
Velocity = displacement ÷ time – size and direction.
A car going round a bend at a steady 20 m/s has constant speed but changing velocity.
questions.label: 1. What is the difference between speed and velocity?
questions.tip: Velocity changes if either the speed or the direction changes.

similar.q: A uniformly accelerated motion has a constant  A) speed.  B) velocity.  C) momentum.  D) acceleration.  E) kinetic energy.
similar.a: D. acceleration. — Because velocity changes, speed, momentum (mv) and kinetic energy also change. Answer: D.

questions.q: A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed?
why: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
questions.label: 2. A runner covers 100 m in 20 s. What is the average speed?
questions.tip: Always divide the TOTAL distance by the TOTAL time.

similar.q: A teacher with a motorbike travelled 40 km for 1 h along a straight road. He took 20 min rest and again travelled 20 km for 2 h along the same straight road. The teacher's average speed, in km/h, is  A) 9.  B) 18.  C) 20.  D) 30.  E) 50.
similar.a: B. 18. — Average speed = 60 ÷ 3.333 = 18 km/h. Answer: B. (Ignoring the rest gives 60 ÷ 3 = 20 km/h – option C, a common trap.)

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m (g = 10 m/s²). How long does it take to reach the ground?
why: Use s = ut + ½gt² with u = 0.
20 m = 0 + ½ × 10 m/s² × t² = 5t².
t² = 4 s², so t = 2 s.

similar.q: A 1 kg mass of cotton, a 2 kg mass of feather and a 3 kg mass of iron are released from a tower of 20 m height at the same time. Neglecting air resistance which one will hit the ground first?  A) Cotton  B) Feather  C) Iron  D) Cotton and feather  E) All hit at the same time.
similar.a: E. All hit at the same time. — All start from rest at the same height, so h = ½gt² gives the same time for all: t = √(2h/g) = √(2 × 20/10) = 2 s. Answer: E.

why: At the top, v = 0. Use v² = u² − 2gh.
questions.label: 9. A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). What maximum height does it reach?

similar.q: Uniform velocity s–t graph?

questions.q: What does the distance–time (s–t) graph look like for uniform velocity?
questions.answer: A straight sloping line; its slope (gradient) is the velocity.
why: Uniform velocity means equal distances in equal times.
So s increases by the same amount each second – a straight line.
Gradient = Δs/Δt = velocity; a steeper line means a larger velocity.
questions.label: 10. What does the distance–time (s–t) graph look like for uniform velocity?
questions.tip: s–t graph: slope = velocity. Horizontal line = at rest.

similar.q: A motor cycle with an initial velocity of 25 m/s accelerates uniformly at a rate of 5 m/s² for 10 seconds. The final velocity of the motor cycle, in m/s, is  A) 20.  B) 30.  C) 50.  D) 75.  E) 100.

questions.q: What does the velocity–time (v–t) graph look like for uniform acceleration?
questions.answer: A straight sloping line; slope = acceleration and area under it = displacement.
why: Uniform acceleration means v changes by the same amount each second.
So the v–t graph is a straight line with gradient Δv/Δt = a.
The area between the line and the time axis gives the displacement.
questions.label: 11. What does the velocity–time (v–t) graph look like for uniform acceleration?
questions.tip: v–t graph: slope = a, area = s.

similar.q: Rest then constant a. s–t shape?

questions.q: An object starts from rest and then has constant acceleration. What shape is its s–t graph?
questions.answer: A curve (parabola) that starts flat and gets steeper.
why: s = ½at² – s depends on t², not t.
At t = 0 the velocity is 0, so the slope starts at zero (flat).
As v increases, the slope increases, giving an upward-curving parabola.
questions.label: 12. An object starts from rest and then has constant acceleration. What shape is its s–t graph?
questions.tip: Curving up on an s–t graph = speeding up.

similar.q: Instantaneous speed from s–t?

questions.q: How do you find instantaneous speed from an s–t graph?
questions.answer: Find the slope of the tangent at that instant.
why: Instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment.
Draw a tangent touching the curve at that time.
Slope of the tangent = Δs/Δt = instantaneous speed.
questions.label: 13. How do you find instantaneous speed from an s–t graph?
questions.tip: Average speed uses a chord between two points; instantaneous uses a tangent.

similar.q: Two baseballs are thrown from the roof of a house with the same initial speed; one is thrown up and the other is thrown down. Compare the speeds of the baseballs just before they hit the ground.  A) The one thrown up has higher speed because the initial velocity is up.  B) The one thrown down has higher speed because the initial velocity is down.  C) They both have the same speed.  D) The one thrown up has higher speed because it has greater acceleration.  E) The one thrown down has higher speed because it has greater acceleration.
similar.a: C. They both have the same speed. — Energy view: same initial KE and same loss of PE → same final KE. The ball thrown up returns to the roof with its initial speed, now downward, and then repeats the other ball's motion. Answer: C.

questions.q: What does a negative velocity mean?
questions.answer: The object moves in the direction opposite to the one chosen as positive.
why: Velocity is a vector; its sign shows direction along a line.
If right/up is chosen as +, a negative velocity means moving left/down.
The sign says nothing about speeding up or slowing down by itself.
questions.label: 14. What does a negative velocity mean?
questions.tip: State your + direction before solving.

similar.q: a=0 means?

questions.q: What does an acceleration of zero mean?
questions.answer: The velocity is constant (which could be zero – at rest).
why: a = Δv/Δt.
If a = 0, then Δv = 0: the velocity does not change.
The object moves at constant velocity or stays at rest.
questions.label: 15. What does an acceleration of zero mean?
questions.tip: a = 0 does not mean v = 0.

similar.q: The velocity of a car increases from 6 m/s to 9 m/s in 5 s. The acceleration of the car, in m/s², is  A) 3.  B) 0.6.  C) 15.  D) 10.8.  E) 1.7.
similar.a: B. 0.6. — a = (9 − 6)/5 = 3/5 = 0.6 m/s². Answer: B. (A, 3, is only the change in velocity.)

questions.q: What is a frame of reference?
questions.answer: The point of view (origin and axes) from which position and motion are measured.
why: Motion is always measured relative to something.
A frame of reference fixes an origin, directions and a clock.
A passenger is at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the road.
questions.label: 16. What is a frame of reference?
questions.tip: Always ask: "moving relative to what?"

similar.q: Car 20 m/s brakes a=−4. Stop distance?

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with acceleration −4 m/s². What is its stopping distance?
why: Use v² = u² + 2as with v = 0.
questions.label: 17. A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with acceleration −4 m/s². What is its stopping distance?
questions.tip: When time is not given or asked, use v² = u² + 2as.

similar.q: Time to stop Q17?

questions.q: For the same car (20 m/s, a = −4 m/s²), how long does it take to stop?
why: Use v = u + at.
questions.label: 18. For the same car (20 m/s, a = −4 m/s²), how long does it take to stop?
questions.tip: Check: average speed 10 m/s × 5 s = 50 m – same as the stopping distance.

similar.q: Area of v–t from 0 to 5s at v=10?

questions.q: A v–t graph shows a constant velocity of 10 m/s from t = 0 to t = 5 s. What is the displacement?
why: Displacement = area under the v–t graph.
The area is a rectangle: height 10 m/s × width 5 s.
questions.label: 19. A v–t graph shows a constant velocity of 10 m/s from t = 0 to t = 5 s. What is the displacement?
questions.tip: Area of a v–t graph = displacement (rectangles, triangles, trapezia).

similar.q: In up-and-down motion problems, what must you choose first?

questions.q: In up-and-down (vertical) motion problems, what must you choose first?
questions.answer: A positive direction – e.g. up = +, so g = −10 m/s².
why: Velocity, displacement and acceleration are vectors with signs.
If up is +, then g acts down, so a = −10 m/s².
Keep the same sign rule for every quantity in the problem.
questions.label: 20. In up-and-down (vertical) motion problems, what must you choose first?
questions.tip: One sign convention per problem – write it at the top.

similar.q: Why is average velocity Δs/Δt, and not the average of the speeds, when an object turns back?

questions.q: Why is average velocity Δs/Δt, and not the average of the speeds, when an object turns back?
questions.answer: Because velocity uses displacement, which can be small (even zero) when the object returns.
why: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time.
When the object turns back, part of the motion cancels, so displacement < distance.
Averaging speeds ignores direction and gives a wrong (too big) value.
questions.label: 21. Why is average velocity Δs/Δt, and not the average of the speeds, when an object turns back?
questions.tip: Round trip back to start: average velocity = 0, average speed > 0.

similar.q: Free fall ignores?

questions.q: What does "free fall" ignore in this chapter?
why: Free fall means the only force is the object's weight.
Then every object accelerates at g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (≈ 10 m/s²), whatever its mass.
Air resistance is ignored in these problems.
questions.label: 22. What does "free fall" ignore in this chapter?
questions.tip: In free fall, a feather and a hammer land together (as on the Moon).

similar.q: Object thrown up, v at same height on way down?

questions.q: An object is thrown up. Compare its velocity when it passes the launch height on the way down with its launch velocity.
why: Without air resistance the motion is symmetric.
Using v² = u² − 2gs with s = 0 (back at launch height) gives v² = u².
So |v| = u, but now it points down: v = −u.
questions.label: 23. An object is thrown up. Compare its velocity when it passes the launch height on the way down with…
questions.tip: Time up = time down, speed up = speed down (no air resistance).

questions.tip: "Metres per second, per second" – velocity changes by so many m/s each second.

similar.q: Trap: why is it wrong to use s = vt when a ≠ 0?
similar.a: That v would have to be average.

questions.q: Trap: why is it wrong to use s = vt when the acceleration is not zero?
questions.answer: s = vt only works with constant velocity; with acceleration you need the average velocity or a suvat equation.
why: When a ≠ 0, v keeps changing, so no single v fits s = vt.
Use s = ((u + v)/2) × t or s = ut + ½at².
Using the final v gives a distance that is too big.
questions.label: 28. Trap: why is it wrong to use s = vt when the acceleration is not zero?
questions.tip: Accelerating? Reach for a suvat equation, not s = vt.

similar.q: Trap: an object is dropped, but a student uses u = 10 m/s. What is wrong?

questions.q: Trap: an object is dropped, but a student uses u = 10 m/s. What is wrong?
questions.answer: A dropped object starts from rest, so u = 0 (10 m/s² is g, not u).
why: "Dropped" or "released" means initial velocity u = 0.
10 is the value of g (an acceleration, m/s²), not a velocity.
